title: Fusion Power: A Clean Energy Breakthrough or an Expensive Gamble?
label: 9 September 2026 · Fusion energy and planning
summary: MPs questioned fusion industry leaders, regulators and the Energy Minister about plans to build Britain's first fusion power stations. Fusion could eventually provide reliable, low-carbon electricity while creating thousands of jobs and valuable UK exports. The Government wants its first prototype power station operating by 2040, while some private companies are aiming for the mid-2030s. Witnesses broadly supported introducing separate planning rules for fusion because its safety risks differ from conventional nuclear power. However, MPs challenged optimistic cost predictions, questioned water use and radioactive waste, and raised unresolved issues about insurance, compensation and local communities' influence over developments. The central message was that fusion offers major opportunities, but its commercial success, future costs and contribution to Britain's electricity supply remain uncertain.

chapters.title: 1. Will communities welcome fusion power?
chapters.takeaway: The West Burton project has received encouraging local support, but MPs questioned whether communities would have a genuine choice about hosting future fusion plants.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Communities that have hosted conventional nuclear power stations are often more willing to accept new ones. Will fusion plants need to be built in those same places?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: Our experience suggests not. West Burton was chosen for STEP in 2022 after communities volunteered to host it. There's never been a nuclear power station there, but the area has a long history of producing electricity. People have welcomed the prospect of new jobs and investment. I think they also recognise that nuclear fusion works differently from nuclear fission and carries different risks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We've previously found serious problems with how energy developers consult local communities. What have you learned at West Burton?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: You need to speak to people early, keep talking and genuinely listen. Consultation shouldn't just be something you do to satisfy a requirement. Residents have raised concerns, particularly about construction traffic, and they've suggested useful solutions. Their involvement improves the project. Being open and honest from the start also helps avoid delays and rising costs.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: But does that mean communities can choose whether to accept a fusion plant? Or could the Government eventually force one on them?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: We want communities to actively welcome these projects, especially because of the economic benefits. Ultimately, government policy could lead to a development going ahead without everyone's agreement. But forcing something through too early, against substantial local opposition, could be counterproductive. We don't expect that situation at West Burton.

chapters.title: 2. How clean and safe would fusion really be?
chapters.takeaway: Fusion could produce low-carbon electricity with different and generally lower nuclear risks than fission, but construction, waste and cooling water still need careful management.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: How environmentally friendly will fusion be compared with conventional nuclear power?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: We expect it to be a very low-carbon source of energy. The fuel comes from materials including lithium and deuterium, which can be obtained from seawater. Generating the electricity itself doesn't release carbon dioxide, although building the plant and producing materials certainly creates emissions. At West Burton, we're reusing an old coal power station site and exploring whether its waste ash can be turned into concrete for construction.

turns.speaker: Jo Nettleton
turns.text: Fusion also has different safety risks. Unlike conventional nuclear fission, it doesn't depend on a continuing chain reaction of splitting atoms. We expect its radioactive waste to be less problematic than the very long-lasting waste from fission. But the technology is still developing. We may encounter new kinds of radioactive or hazardous waste that need suitable ways of being handled and disposed of. There's also the ordinary environmental impact of building a large industrial site.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: Could fusion plants be small enough to build in lots of different places?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: STEP is expected to be a prototype of around 100 megawatts. Our current thinking favours large plants that could provide continuous electricity or supply major industries. Making small fusion reactors may be difficult, although private companies might find approaches we haven't considered. It's too early to know what sizes will become commercially practical.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: I'm concerned about water. We're already being told Britain needs more reservoirs. How much additional demand would fusion create?

turns.speaker: Jo Nettleton
turns.text: The water requirement at West Burton won't be insignificant, but we expect it to be much smaller than at a large conventional nuclear station such as Hinkley Point C. We'll need to consider the combined demand from fusion, data centres and other developments planned in the area. The precise requirements are still being worked out.

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: Much of the water is needed for cooling and would be returned rather than permanently consumed. One important issue is how much warmer that returned water would be. Developers must calculate their expected water use and show how they'll manage its effects before their projects can proceed.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: Who actually regulates these plants? I thought the aim was to simplify nuclear regulation.

turns.speaker: Jo Nettleton
turns.text: The Environment Agency will oversee environmental issues, while the Health and Safety Executive will regulate industrial safety. Fusion has a simpler regulatory arrangement than fission because the underlying physical risks are different. That doesn't mean fusion is simple technology or free from hazards. We already regulate fusion research at Culham, and we're developing the expertise needed for larger plants.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: We've heard fusion described as having zero carbon emissions. Is that really accurate when you consider the materials that must be mined, transported and manufactured?

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: No energy technology has absolutely zero emissions throughout its entire life. Fusion doesn't release carbon dioxide when generating power, but construction and its supply chain do produce emissions. The correct description is low-carbon electricity, comparable in that respect to nuclear fission or offshore wind.

chapters.title: 3. Planning permission, radioactive materials and insurance
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses argued that separate planning rules would help fusion projects progress, while insisting that existing safety laws cover radioactive materials; compensation arrangements still need development.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Why give fusion its own planning rules instead of using the system for conventional nuclear stations? Those existing sites already have trained workers, electricity connections and local acceptance.

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: They're different technologies with different risks. Having a separate national policy statement, EN-8, gives developers and investors a clearer understanding of how fusion projects will be assessed. It also helps reassure communities that they're not being asked to approve conventional nuclear technology under another name. Private companies are already considering where to build their first commercial plants.

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: We shouldn't restrict ourselves to existing nuclear sites. The opportunity isn't just to produce electricity for Britain. We already have substantial wind and other energy resources. The larger opportunity is to become a leading exporter of fusion technology worldwide. Different safety requirements mean we can consider places such as West Burton without taking sites away from future fission projects.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Fusion needs tritium, which is radioactive. Initially it would have to be imported, wouldn't it? Why doesn't the planning policy specifically address its transport, storage and use?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: The initial supply would need to be imported. Our aim is for operating reactors to produce their own tritium using lithium. Britain already imports smaller quantities from Canada. There are existing laws covering radioactive materials, including their transport, so those risks aren't being ignored simply because the planning document doesn't describe every requirement.

turns.speaker: Jo Nettleton
turns.text: Tritium is covered by rules for radioactive substances. The Environment Agency and Health and Safety Executive deal with different aspects of operating fusion facilities, while the Office for Nuclear Regulation oversees transport of radioactive materials. Planning permission is only the first step. Developers must also satisfy the relevant safety and environmental regulators.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: That's now three regulators, which doesn't sound especially simple. And if something goes wrong, who compensates people affected by radiation?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: The compensation and insurance arrangements still need work. We start from the principle that developers should pay for harm they cause. But fusion is a new industry, and the Government is examining what insurance arrangements might be appropriate and whether some changes will be needed to help the market develop.

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: We believe fusion risks can be insured by private companies. Insurance products specifically aimed at fusion are already emerging in the UK. Developing expertise in that area could itself become a business opportunity.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: Would it help to grant development consent with conditions that must be met later?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: Sometimes. A clear condition requiring local apprenticeships or skills training could benefit both the developer and the community. But overly restrictive conditions can slow a project down. The important thing is that developers know what's expected. Conditions should resolve uncertainty rather than create more of it.

turns.speaker: Jo Nettleton
turns.text: One issue we particularly want strengthened is flood protection. These plants may operate for a very long time, and flood risks could change substantially during that period. Developers need to consider those future risks from the beginning, not only what the site looks like today.

chapters.title: 4. Can fusion become affordable, and can Britain lead?
chapters.takeaway: Private companies are targeting competitive electricity prices, but those figures remain unproven, and the witnesses stressed that sustained investment is essential if Britain wants to profit from fusion.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: You say fusion is getting close to commercial use. What would its electricity cost compared with other technologies?

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: Some of our member companies are targeting roughly £35 to £75 per megawatt-hour. Those are their estimates for plants built after the technology has become established, not for the first experimental power stations. If achieved, that would make fusion competitive with other low-carbon electricity sources. But these are company targets, not proven operating costs.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: The Government is spending £2.5 billion over five years, while countries such as China and America are spending much more in total. Isn't it remarkable to think we could achieve such low costs with that investment?

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: It wouldn't happen through UK public spending alone. Around $15 billion of private investment has gone into fusion companies worldwide over approximately five years. Some companies have signed agreements to supply future electricity to businesses such as Google and Microsoft. International investment and research will matter enormously. These companies also understand that fusion won't succeed commercially if the electricity is too expensive.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Paul, are you expecting electricity from West Burton to cost £35 to £75 per megawatt-hour?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: We don't know. Those are private companies' ambitions, not a forecast for STEP. Our starting point is to make sure fusion works technically and can eventually compete commercially. If it becomes broadly competitive with conventional large nuclear power stations, that would be a promising result, particularly given its different risks and potential to be exported internationally.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Britain has led in technologies before and then failed to benefit commercially. How do we stop that happening again?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: We need sustained Government support, clear planning rules, effective safety regulation and continued research at UKAEA. We also need STEP to help take the technology from laboratory experiments to a working power station, and arrangements that encourage private companies to invest. We can't assume today's scientific lead will automatically become tomorrow's commercial success.

turns.speaker: Wera Hobhouse
turns.text: We can't expect Britain to manufacture every part of a fusion plant. Which areas should we concentrate on?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: One strength is designing all the different systems to work together as a complete power station. Our experience operating JET gives us valuable expertise. We also have strengths in robotics, specialised materials and handling tritium fuel. Another major opportunity is developing ways to produce tritium inside reactors using lithium. Nobody has yet demonstrated the complete process in a commercial power station.

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: We also have strong private companies working on magnets and other specialist equipment. The challenge is getting public laboratories and private businesses to work together so British research becomes products that companies can sell. Stable government policy and international partnerships will make that much easier.

chapters.title: 5. Creating jobs and building an industry
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses saw fusion as a potential source of thousands of skilled jobs, but said firms need confidence that projects will continue before investing heavily in workers and factories.

turns.speaker: Wera Hobhouse
turns.text: Should the Government keep building experimental reactors itself, or concentrate on making it easier for private companies to develop them?

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: Ultimately, we expect fusion to become a private industry. Government research at Culham has been enormously valuable, including work on robotics and materials. The difficult part now is helping businesses turn that research into commercial products and keeping as much of the resulting industry in Britain as possible.

turns.speaker: Wera Hobhouse
turns.text: What will give companies the confidence to invest in training people for an industry that doesn't really exist yet?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: That's one of the reasons Government investment matters. Building an initial plant creates real demand for equipment and skilled workers. Suppliers can then justify hiring staff and training apprentices. Universities and colleges can develop courses around the skills employers will actually need. Some expertise overlaps with conventional nuclear power, but areas such as the physics of fusion are different.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: Other new industries have struggled because they didn't plan for the workforce early enough. How will you avoid that?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: We're trying to forecast the jobs we'll need years ahead. The most immediate shortages aren't necessarily scientists. Right now, we particularly need people with commercial and project management expertise. Later, construction workers could become the biggest shortage. We've already engaged with around 16,000 people in the West Burton area, including thousands of schoolchildren, and we're working with local education providers.

turns.speaker: Jo Nettleton
turns.text: That early contact with communities matters for recruitment too. Young people are much more likely to consider careers in engineering, science or regulation if they understand what's being developed near them and can see opportunities for themselves.

turns.speaker: Tris Denton
turns.text: People also need confidence that they can build a lasting career. A single exciting project might attract someone temporarily. Several projects, with more work expected afterwards, give people confidence that they can support their families by staying in the industry.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: How many jobs might fusion create over the next decade?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: At West Burton alone, we expect around 1,500 people to operate the plant, with construction employment potentially reaching about 8,000 at its peak. Those figures don't include the businesses we'd like to attract nearby. Across the country, companies supplying fusion plants could create tens of thousands of additional jobs if the industry succeeds.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How much of this is publicly funded, and how do we ensure that private investors don't take the benefits overseas?

turns.speaker: Paul Methven
turns.text: STEP is currently fully government-funded, but we spend much of that money through private industry. Our partnership with Tokamak Energy on magnets is one example. We're examining future private investment while making sure Britain keeps the economic benefits. The bigger goal is a British network of suppliers that can sell equipment and expertise worldwide.

chapters.title: 6. Why the Government wants separate planning rules
chapters.takeaway: The Minister defended creating a dedicated fusion planning policy to attract investment and prepare for projects, while acknowledging concerns about complexity and local control.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Minister, when will fusion actually produce electricity, and what price should we expect?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: We don't have definite answers yet. Our aim is to have the first STEP plant operating by 2040, hopefully earlier. We're closer than ever to making fusion a practical source of electricity, but it hasn't yet been produced commercially. I wouldn't commit to a particular price before we've built the technology. Early plants will also teach us how to make later ones cheaper.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why do we need another national policy statement when we already have planning policies covering other forms of energy?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: Because fusion and fission are fundamentally different, especially when it comes to safety and radioactive materials. We already have general planning rules for energy infrastructure, but fusion needs some specific considerations. EN-8 should make clear what developers must do before seeking permission. We want that clarity in place before applications start arriving, rather than having planning delays hold up the technology.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Won't creating separate policies for more technologies make the planning system increasingly complicated?

turns.speaker: David Sandford
turns.text: We don't want a separate document for every technology. Each case should be assessed individually, and a new statement should only be created when there's a particular need.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: What's made a dedicated fusion policy necessary now? Is this partly about persuading international companies to invest here?

turns.speaker: David Sandford
turns.text: Absolutely. We have STEP moving forward, but we're also hearing from private fusion companies, including American businesses, that are deciding where to build new facilities. They see Britain as a possible destination. They tell us that clear planning and safety rules matter when deciding where to invest.

turns.speaker: Claire Young
turns.text: Even smaller fusion projects could ask to use the national planning system. Doesn't that risk taking decisions away from local communities? And why are the thresholds different in England and Wales?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: Projects of 50 megawatts or more in England, and 350 megawatts or more in Wales, fall within the national system. Wales has a higher threshold because of decisions made with the Welsh Government. Some smaller projects could still be nationally important. We also have to recognise that local planning departments may lack experience of fusion, so a national process may be more suitable for certain developments.

turns.speaker: Claire Young
turns.text: But will the people examining those national applications understand the technology? And what support will local planning officers receive?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: The Planning Inspectorate needs trained specialists before the first applications arrive. We're bringing the policy forward early partly to allow that preparation. Local planning departments also need more staff and training. The Government has invested in both, and I can provide the Committee with further details.

chapters.title: 7. Challenging the Government on safety and compensation
chapters.takeaway: MPs pressed the Minister over radioactive material, insurance and responsibility for accidents; he defended the existing safety rules but acknowledged that insurance arrangements are still developing.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: We've heard concerns that EN-8 doesn't say enough about radioactive waste and how radioactive materials will be stored. Do you think anything important is missing?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: No. The statement addresses the storage and processing of radioactive material and waste, and other established laws cover transport and storage. Planning policy doesn't need to repeat every safety requirement. These are separate legal processes that developers must follow.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: But an insurance organisation at Lloyd's has warned that the policy needs strengthening. It wants developers to assess all the radioactive material, stored energy and possible ways an accident might release dangerous substances, together. Who would pay compensation if people were harmed? I'm concerned you haven't properly addressed this evidence.

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: I haven't read that particular submission, although officials examine the evidence received. Public confidence in safety is essential. Our assessment is that fusion carries considerably lower risks than conventional nuclear power. We therefore expect it to be covered through more ordinary industrial insurance arrangements, rather than the special arrangements used for fission. But the insurance market is still developing.

turns.speaker: David Sandford
turns.text: Developers will have to produce safety assessments for the Health and Safety Executive. That's separate from the planning decision. We're talking regularly with insurers so they can assess fusion's particular risks and decide how to cover them. It's an area where discussions are still at an early stage.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: Insurers might find that response rather patronising. They're the people who should be assessing these risks and deciding what it costs to insure against them. On planning, wouldn't attaching conditions to permission create just as many delays as waiting for all the safety issues to be settled?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: Conditions can be useful when they address a clear concern, including something important to local communities. But they should be relatively rare. Investors need to know what will be required of them. If conditions become unpredictable or excessive, they can increase costs and cause the very delays we're trying to avoid.

turns.speaker: Sir Christopher Chope
turns.text: If the technology won't be ready for years, are we trying to anticipate too many problems now?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: Construction work will begin well before the technology is fully ready. We're aiming for an operational plant by 2040 and hope to achieve that sooner. Preparing the planning system now should help us avoid the years of unnecessary delay that have affected other major infrastructure projects.

chapters.title: 8. Where fusion fits into Britain's energy future
chapters.takeaway: The Minister presented fusion as a long-term addition to renewable and conventional nuclear power, not a replacement for them, with its strongest immediate benefits in research, jobs and exports.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: Is fusion really necessary for Britain's energy security? Wouldn't it be better to spend more on technologies that already work, such as offshore wind? Other developing technologies need support too.

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: We can have energy security without fusion, but we need a mixture of technologies. Wind and solar are important, although their output changes with the weather. Conventional nuclear power, and potentially fusion, can provide electricity more consistently. We're also supporting other technologies, including floating offshore wind, hydrogen and carbon capture. Fusion isn't replacing those investments.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: The Government seems extremely enthusiastic about fusion, despite it not being commercially proven. Is £2.5 billion really the right amount to spend?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: We think it's an appropriate amount to keep the research progressing and encourage private investment. But supporting research doesn't mean we'll build unlimited fusion plants regardless of cost. When commercial projects become possible, affordability will be central to those decisions.

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: Will fusion face the same problems getting connected to the electricity network as other energy projects? And are you sure it isn't being presented as a solution to all our energy problems?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: Fusion won't get special treatment when it comes to grid connections. West Burton has an advantage because the former coal power station already has a connection. We're working to address wider delays across the electricity network. And no, fusion isn't the answer to everything. We'll still need wind, solar and conventional nuclear power for the foreseeable future. Fusion's contribution will develop over time.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: We've previously heard that fusion might provide only 10% of Britain's energy needs by 2100. Isn't that underwhelming?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: I haven't seen that particular calculation, so I can't judge it. Our first plant will produce relatively little electricity, but it will be a starting point. Research has advanced faster in recent years than many people expected. Future progress could allow us to be more ambitious, although we can't know that yet.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Are we ahead of America and China? And should we worry about other countries stealing technology or undermining our energy security?

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: Britain genuinely leads in important areas, but I wouldn't claim we're ahead of every other country. International research partnerships are essential, and we're working with countries including America and Canada. We also take threats to our technology and energy infrastructure seriously. With China, our approach is to cooperate where possible while protecting national security.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Which parts of the industry could Britain realistically dominate, and are regulators doing enough to encourage British manufacturing?

turns.speaker: David Sandford
turns.text: We're particularly strong at designing how every part of a fusion station fits together. We also have expertise in powerful magnets, robotics and advanced materials. Those are areas where British companies could supply equipment and technology to projects around the world.

turns.speaker: Michael Shanks
turns.text: We should do more to build these industries in Britain. I've told Ofgem, the energy regulator, that supporting economic growth could be stronger in its work. But there's a difficult balance: we want British manufacturing and jobs, while also keeping energy bills affordable. With offshore wind, we missed opportunities to establish more manufacturing here early on. Fusion gives us a chance to get that right from the beginning.
